finding: Migration at the long-run average raises GDP per person, mainly because migrants are younger
unit: % of GDP per person (about $7,000 a person in 2013-14 dollars)
comparison: NOM at the long-term historical average vs zero NOM
source: Productivity Commission (2016), Migrant intake into Australia (Inquiry Report No. 77; dated 13 April, released 12 September 2016)
caveats: Assumes the intake keeps its young age profile. Does not count congestion, environmental or housing costs

finding: Share of the population aged 65 and over
source: Productivity Commission (2016), Migrant intake into Australia (Inquiry Report No. 77; dated 13 April, released 12 September 2016)
caveats: Migration delays ageing but does not stop it

topic: Wages and jobs of existing workers
finding: Recent immigrants had a negligible effect on the wages, employment and participation of existing workers at the aggregate level
comparison: Econometric analysis commissioned for the inquiry
source: Productivity Commission (2016), Migrant intake into Australia (Inquiry Report No. 77; dated 13 April, released 12 September 2016)
caveats: Effects can be concentrated among lower-skilled and young workers

finding: Lifetime fiscal cost of a parent visa holder, per adult
source: Productivity Commission (2016), Migrant intake into Australia (Inquiry Report No. 77; dated 13 April, released 12 September 2016)
caveats: Older arrivals use more health care and work less

caveats: As reported by SBS; check IGR Appendix A4 (sensitivity analysis)

finding: Higher migration (285,000 a year) raises gross national income per person only slightly
source: The Treasury (2026, September 21), 2026 Intergenerational Report, as reported by SBS News (2026, September 23), The numbers raising new questions about Australia's future wealth
caveats: As reported by SBS; check IGR Appendix A4

finding: Old-age dependency ratio (people 65+ per 100 of working age)
source: The Treasury (2026, September 21), 2026 Intergenerational Report, as reported by SBS News (2026, September 23), The numbers raising new questions about Australia's future wealth
caveats: As reported by SBS; the ABC's IGR story gives about 29 now and 39 by 2066 on another definition. Check IGR Appendix A4

finding: Lower migration raises gross debt: about 32.2% of GDP instead of 27.4%
source: The Treasury (2026, September 21), 2026 Intergenerational Report, as reported by Commins, P. (2026, September 21), Think Australia would be better off with less migration? The numbers tell a different story, The Guardian (read via inkl)
caveats: SBS says 'rise by 4.8 per cent'. 27.4% is the Treasurer's baseline; 32.2% is The Guardian's figure. The Guardian also says 'nearly 10 percentage points', which does not fit. Check IGR Appendix A4

finding: The 2005-2018 population surge (adult population 3.3% higher by 2018) left real rents higher than otherwise
comparison: Population growth rising from 1.5% (2005) to a 2.4% peak (2008) vs staying at 1.5%
source: Saunders, T., & Tulip, P. (2019), A model of the Australian housing market (RBA Research Discussion Paper 2019-01)
caveats: Prices follow rents gradually. Larger than many local studies find; effects grow with geographic scale

topic: Wages and jobs of existing workers
finding: Review of Australian studies: effects on existing workers' earnings are modest and generally positive
unit: % earnings change per 1% increase in immigrants in a skill group (foreign-born population in Bond and Gaston; immigrant share in Kifle)
source: Brell, C., & Dustmann, C. (2019), Immigration and wage growth: The case of Australia, in RBA Conference Volume 2019
caveats: Some negative effects for workers with vocational qualifications, but not robust

finding: Average household size; at 2.8 people per home Australia would need 1.2 million fewer dwellings
